script: They begged me after everyone bailed—my refusal turned their wedding into chaos.. I was 24, a girl who had already dropped a decent chunk of cash on my bestie's wedding—like, enough to make the venue look lit. I'd also been on standby for errands, setting up the table, that whole "I am here for the day" vibe. (Honestly, I was practically a wedding DJ in my head.) Then, a few weeks before the big day, the groomsmen who'd promised to chip in for the bachelor party, some décor, and a few group gifts suddenly bailed. The friend who's tying the knot asked me if I'd cover the gaps so nothing got scaled back. The amount wasn't a fortune, but it wasn't a tiny change either. It'd mean dipping into the savings I was stacking for my own goals—like the new apartment, that travel fund, the new laptop. I said, "No jerks here, I can't be the backup wallet when others drop out." I still offered my time and labor, but no cash. My friend looked crushed, said they felt let down. Then the group chat exploded. "You're abandoning them on their biggest day?" "Are you even a real friend if you won't step up financially?" The drama was the usual loyalty test—like, who's actually in this for the long haul? (I know, right?) I am not the type to become the default safety net when people bail. I already gave what I could, and I was ready to roll up my sleeves. If I kept pulling money out, I'd be sacrificing my own future. That's not friendship; that's debt. The stakes? My own savings, my own plans, my sanity. I couldn't let a wedding dictate my financial freedom. So, am I the jerk? No. I am the friend who sets boundaries and keeps my own life on track. If that makes anyone mad, that's their problem, not mine.
